expectedText:
H-1B VISA SPONSORSHIP COMPLIANCE — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

ABOUT THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet summarizes federal obligations that apply when Acme, Inc. sponsors Jordan Lee for H-1B nonimmigrant work authorization for the position of Software Engineer. It describes requirements under the Immigration and Nationality Act's Labor Condition Application (LCA) provisions, 8 U.S.C. § 1182(n), and the Department of Labor's implementing wage regulation, 20 C.F.R. § 655.731. It states facts about these federal requirements; it does not instruct Acme, Inc. or Jordan Lee on how to respond to their particular circumstances, and it is not a substitute for the LCA and petition documents themselves.

LCA WAGE ATTESTATION REQUIREMENT
Before an H-1B nonimmigrant may be admitted or provided status in an occupational classification, the sponsoring employer must file a Labor Condition Application (LCA) attesting that it is offering and will offer wages that are at least the greater of two figures: the actual wage level the employer pays to other individuals with similar experience and qualifications for the same specific employment, or the prevailing wage level for the occupational classification in the area of employment. The employer must also attest that it will provide working conditions for the H-1B worker that will not adversely affect the working conditions of workers similarly employed.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "the actual wage level paid by the employer to all other individuals with similar experience and qualifications for the specific employment in question"
  — 8 U.S.C. § 1182(n)(1)(A)(i)(I) (Cornell LII text), 8 U.S.C. § 1182(n)(1)(A)(i)(I) (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/8/1182)
  "the prevailing wage level for the occupational classification in the area of employment"
  — 8 U.S.C. § 1182(n)(1)(A)(i)(II) (Cornell LII text), 8 U.S.C. § 1182(n)(1)(A)(i)(II) (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/8/1182)
  "will provide working conditions for such a nonimmigrant that will not adversely affect the working conditions of workers similarly employed."
  — 8 U.S.C. § 1182(n)(1)(A)(ii) (Cornell LII text), 8 U.S.C. § 1182(n)(1)(A)(ii) (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/8/1182)
  Known gap: The statute states the wage floor as a comparison of two figures determined at the time the LCA is filed; it does not itself specify the methodology for calculating the prevailing wage or actual wage — that methodology, along with permissible wage sources, is set out separately in the Department of Labor's implementing regulation at 20 C.F.R. § 655.731(a), not in the statutory text quoted here.

LCA NOTICE REQUIREMENT
At the time an LCA is filed, the employer must also attest that it has provided notice of the filing. If a bargaining representative exists for the employer's employees in the occupational classification and area for which H-1B workers are sought, notice must go to that representative. If there is no bargaining representative, the employer must instead provide notice through methods such as physical posting in conspicuous locations at the place of employment, or electronic notification to employees in that occupational classification.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "has provided notice of the filing under this paragraph to the bargaining representative (if any) of the employer’s employees in the occupational classification and area for which aliens are sought"
  — 8 U.S.C. § 1182(n)(1)(C)(i) (Cornell LII text), 8 U.S.C. § 1182(n)(1)(C)(i) (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/8/1182)
  "if there is no such bargaining representative, has provided notice of filing in the occupational classification through such methods as physical posting in conspicuous locations at the place of employment or electronic notification to employees in the occupational classification for which H–1B nonimmigrants are sought."
  — 8 U.S.C. § 1182(n)(1)(C)(ii) (Cornell LII text), 8 U.S.C. § 1182(n)(1)(C)(ii) (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/8/1182)
  Known gap: The statute names physical posting and electronic notification as illustrative methods ("such methods as") rather than an exclusive list, and it does not itself specify posting duration, content, or location requirements — those operational details are set by Department of Labor regulation (20 C.F.R. § 655.734) rather than by the statutory text quoted here.

DETERMINING THE REQUIRED WAGE
Department of Labor regulations implementing the LCA wage attestation specify that the required wage is the greater of the actual wage rate or the prevailing wage, and that this required wage generally must be paid to the H-1B worker in cash, in hand, free and clear, when due. A cash wage below the required wage level is permitted only to the extent a deduction from wages qualifies as an authorized deduction under the regulation's separate deduction criteria.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "that is, that the wage shall be the greater of the actual wage rate (as specified in paragraph (a)(1) of this section) or the prevailing wage (as specified in paragraph (a)(2) of this section)"
  — 20 C.F.R. § 655.731(a) (eCFR text), 20 C.F.R. § 655.731(a) (https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-20/chapter-V/part-655/subpart-H/section-655.731)
  "The required wage must be paid to the employee, cash in hand, free and clear, when due, except that deductions made in accordance with paragraph (c)(9) of this section may reduce the cash wage below the level of the required wage."
  — 20 C.F.R. § 655.731(c)(1) (eCFR text), 20 C.F.R. § 655.731(c)(1) (https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-20/chapter-V/part-655/subpart-H/section-655.731)
  Known gap: This clause states the general cash-in-hand rule and its stated exception for authorized deductions; it does not itself catalog which deductions qualify as authorized (for example, legally required withholding, or deductions meeting the regulation's voluntary-authorization and benefit-of-employee criteria) — those criteria appear in a separate paragraph of the same regulation, addressed in the next clause below.

NO RECOUPMENT OF ATTORNEY FEES OR H-1B FILING COSTS
Department of Labor regulations governing the H-1B required wage treat attorney fees and other costs connected to performing H-1B program functions the employer is required to perform — such as preparing and filing the LCA and the H-1B petition — as the employer's own business expense. A wage deduction may not be used to recoup that business expense, whether the deduction is one that would otherwise be authorized because it is customary in the occupation or area of employment, or one that would otherwise be authorized because the employee voluntarily agreed to it in writing.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "except that the deduction may not recoup a business expense(s) of the employer (including attorney fees and other costs connected to the performance of H-1B program functions which are required to be performed by the employer, e.g., preparation and filing of LCA and H-1B petition)"
  — 20 C.F.R. § 655.731(c)(9)(ii) (eCFR text), 20 C.F.R. § 655.731(c)(9)(ii) (https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-20/chapter-V/part-655/subpart-H/section-655.731)
  "Is not a recoupment of the employer's business expense (e.g., tools and equipment; transportation costs where such transportation is an incident of, and necessary to, the employment; living expenses when the employee is traveling on the employer's business; attorney fees and other costs connected to the performance of H-1B program functions which are required to be performed by the employer (e.g., preparation and filing of LCA and H-1B petition))"
  — 20 C.F.R. § 655.731(c)(9)(iii)(C) (eCFR text), 20 C.F.R. § 655.731(c)(9)(iii)(C) (https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-20/chapter-V/part-655/subpart-H/section-655.731)
  Known gap: This no-recoupment rule is a limit on what counts as an authorized wage deduction under two separate criteria sets in the same subsection (20 C.F.R. § 655.731(c)(9)(ii) and (c)(9)(iii)(C)) — it is not a single freestanding prohibition codified in one subsection, and it does not by its terms reach costs an employee pays out of pocket rather than through a wage deduction, or costs that are not connected to functions the employer itself is required to perform.

PENALTIES VERSUS LIQUIDATED DAMAGES FOR EARLY DEPARTURE
Separately from the attorney-fee recoupment rule, Department of Labor regulations prohibit an employer from requiring, directly or indirectly, that an H-1B worker pay a penalty for ceasing employment before a date agreed to by the worker and employer, and prohibit any wage deduction made to collect such a penalty. The regulation distinguishes this from bona fide liquidated damages, which an employer is permitted to receive from a departing H-1B worker, provided the deduction otherwise satisfies the regulation's separate authorized-deduction criteria.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "The employer is not permitted to require (directly or indirectly) that the nonimmigrant pay a penalty for ceasing employment with the employer prior to an agreed date. Therefore, the employer shall not make any deduction from or reduction in the payment of the required wage to collect such a penalty."
  — 20 C.F.R. § 655.731(c)(10)(i)(A) (eCFR text), 20 C.F.R. § 655.731(c)(10)(i)(A) (https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-20/chapter-V/part-655/subpart-H/section-655.731)
  "The employer is permitted to receive bona fide liquidated damages from the H-1B nonimmigrant who ceases employment with the employer prior to an agreed date."
  — 20 C.F.R. § 655.731(c)(10)(i)(B) (eCFR text), 20 C.F.R. § 655.731(c)(10)(i)(B) (https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-20/chapter-V/part-655/subpart-H/section-655.731)
  Known gap: Whether a given payment obligation is a prohibited "penalty" or a permitted "liquidated damages" provision is determined under applicable state contract law, not by a federal test stated in this regulation — the regulation identifies the distinction and points to state law to draw it, so the classification of any particular provision cannot be determined from the federal text alone.

NO REBATE OF THE EMPLOYER'S ACWIA FILING FEE
Department of Labor regulations separately prohibit an employer from receiving, and an H-1B worker from paying, any part of the additional $500 or $1,000 filing fee the employer owes under section 214(c) of the Immigration and Nationality Act, whether the payment would run directly or indirectly, voluntarily or involuntarily.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "The employer may not receive, and the H-1B nonimmigrant may not pay, any part of the $500 additional filing fee (for a petition filed prior to December 18, 2000) or $1,000 additional filing fee (for a petition filed on or subsequent to December 18, 2000), whether directly or indirectly, voluntarily or involuntarily."
  — 20 C.F.R. § 655.731(c)(10)(ii) (eCFR text), 20 C.F.R. § 655.731(c)(10)(ii) (https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-20/chapter-V/part-655/subpart-H/section-655.731)
  Known gap: This rule addresses only the employer's own statutory ACWIA/fraud-prevention filing fee under INA § 214(c); it does not address other filing fees associated with an H-1B petition (such as the base I-129 filing fee or premium processing fee), and current fee amounts should be confirmed against U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services' fee schedule in effect at the time of filing rather than assumed from this regulation's stated dollar figures.

RECORDKEEPING AND FURTHER INFORMATION
Acme, Inc. is required to maintain documentation supporting the wage statement and wage payments described above for as long as required by federal regulation, and to make certain records available for public examination. This information sheet reflects the LCA wage, notice, and deduction provisions described above as of September 1, 2026; it does not address every LCA attestation or every H-1B compliance obligation, including obligations that apply specifically to H-1B-dependent employers or employers with a history of willful violations.
